utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, good afternoon everyone in the Court. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On Wednesday, the 17th of October, I'd like to greet Mr. Stringer, the Defence teams and the accused. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, there are several issues we should deal with. I have noticed that Mr. Coric is absent. What has happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we haven't received information of any kind so far that I assume that it's because he occasionally feels ill. He has high pressure sometimes but at the moment I'm not sure what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber hopes that he will be feeling better rapidly. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for taking up your time but I think the two minutes will be quite sufficient. In your decision of the 4th of October 2007, you ordered the Defence to inform the Prosecution by the 17th of October 2007 about the Defence's intentions to use an alibi defence. Your Honours, if I could have until the next week, I would be very grateful because we don't have all the documents we need. We are still waiting for some of them to arrive and we would like to prepare this as best as possible. Naturally, I can provide you with such information and then add supplements or additional information but I don't think that would be a useful way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I have understood you correctly, you are requesting two additional weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the utmost. One week extra should be sufficient, since I'm a little ill now, well, if you give me two weeks, I'll be very happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have already spoken to my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, and we have provided you information about the same subject but we mentioned the period concerned alone and the reason for which we believe that an alibi was at stake but we would also require additional time to collect evidence pursuant to Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, we haven't forgotten you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is an issue which directly affects the rights of the Prosecution and its entitlement to a fair trial as well. Two weeks as a maximum, I find myself it's difficult to object but at the same time, you know, the Defence have had years really to -- of notice, of what are the crimes and the locations and the dates and it's all in the indictment. It's not clear to me why the Defence are not in a position now as opposed to two weeks from now in order to inform themselves and the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution as to the nature of any special defences. We are in the Trial Chamber's hands on this decision, but if this deadline of today is going to be extended, Mr. President, our request is that it be a short extension of two weeks at the maximum, possibly even one week, and that it be a firm deadline. That is to say, that if the deadline is not met, then those -- the Defence will be under the rule not entitled to call alibi witnesses or in our interpretation of the rule to put on alibi evidence beyond the accused giving testimony about that which we recognise they can always do, but we think that if the deadline is not met, then a firm ruling has to be made excluding any other evidence about alibis and special defences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated and given that Mr. Kovacic was ill for a period of time, and the Defence needs some time to collect more documents, the Chamber will grant the Defence an additional week which means that the deadline will be the 24th of October. So you have one additional week. Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. One very brief matter on behalf, I understand, of all the accused and Defence counsel in this case. There has been some consultation with my learned friend for the Prosecution. As I understand the Court schedule at the moment, the Court will break for the Christmas recess on the 13th of December and I understand that any 98 bis motions that any Defence team wishes to make will be argued on the 7th of January. Your Honour, that's quite close upon the 13th of December. There is no objection from the Prosecution, indeed I understand they support the Defence application to extend the date so that any 98 bis motions that may be argued by any accused be argued on the 21st of January. Your Honour, this may have at least two advantages, in the event that any applications for provisional release are made and granted, it may assist the Court administration in deciding its schedule, but in addition, it would allow the Defence to focus its submissions. Of course, in the bad old days of submissions of no case to answer or 98 bis, everything was thrown into the melting pot and that was one reason why the oral application was amended so that Defence counsel really focus submissions to those of merit given the lower threshold of proof. Your Honour, I think the additional time would allow a very hard-working Defence team for the accused that have been in this case time to take a little break over Christmas and, of course, to prepare this matter so that they can do justice to it, and assist Your Honours in determining whether or not any application that is made is properly grounded and I think Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- will speak for himself. I'm sure the Prosecution, those that celebrate Christmas, would also be grateful for a few days with their families instead of working incessantly throughout that period. Your Honour, that is the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Khan has accurately represented the position of the Prosecution. We have indeed conferred and the Prosecution would not object, in fact we would support, an application to extend by two weeks the timing of the 98 bis submissions from the 7th of January to the 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate tomorrow. We will be meeting tomorrow. And we'll deliberate and next time we see each other we'll tell you about our decision. As far as I'm concerned, there is a scheduling order, and this scheduling order has been subject of many discussions within the Chamber, and we took all the various elements into consideration. We have listened to the application made. We have taken note of the Prosecution's position, and we will inform you of our decision in due course. Since we are dealing with the schedule, I can tie this up with another problem, another issue that I wanted to raise. Next week, Wednesday is a holiday and the Chamber has decided that in order to allow everyone to have a break after this diabolical rhythm since August we have decided to not have a hearing on Thursday, and thus, Wednesday -- a witness will be coming on Monday and Tuesday. The witness for the 22nd and 23rd of October has been scheduled for a long time and I have discovered that the witness in question will not be appearing. I don't know the reason for which this witness will not be appearing, if he is ill I understand that he can't come, but if that is not the case, there is no reason for the witness not to appear, and if the witness is creating difficulties, we can issue a subpoena, a summons, for Monday, which means that the witness could catch a plane on Saturday morning to get here. Mr. Stringer, why is this witness not coming here on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that we briefly go into private session? It might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, I'll give you the floor because there are several IC numbers we have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. OTP has submitted its response to Defence exhibits tendered through Miroslav Rupcic. The list submitted by OTP has been given IC 694. One of the parties have also submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Ray Lane. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number 695. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the usher now bring the witness into the courtroom? According to our calculations, the legal officer has informed us that the Praljak Defence has an hour and the Petkovic Defence also has one hour at its disposal. That should be the case if the Judges haven't made a mistake. Mr. Kovacic, I believe, that Mr. Praljak will be conducting the cross-examination. He's ready. He has his maps, he has the lectern. Inform us very rapidly of the exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right. You've seen the documents. You are familiar with the facts. He was there at the time. You know all the details of the situation. So I believe that situation is in accordance with your decision and as a result, Praljak should be granted leave to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, commander, and I apologise for having made you wait but we had to deal with certain procedural matters before calling you into the courtroom. Now that we have done that, we can commence with the cross-examination and its General Praljak who will be cross-examining you in person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Lane. Mr. Lane, due to our limited time available, and I will be dealing with questions on the map, could you please answer as briefly as possible. If Their Honours require more extensive explanations or additional explanations, they will ask you for them. As far as this part of my cross-examination is concerned, I would just like us to look into the kind of information there was on the ground, the information you had at your disposal and what the basic essential facts are. So could you give us the kind of answers that a professional officer is expected to give. My first question: During your stay or tour of duty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you ever meet with me?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's a very, very good question. I think I met with you on one occasion but I cannot be sure. If you're hair was black in 1992 it's a very strong possibility I met you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's a difficult answer. Could you please tell me when you think that was and where it was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been very, very early on in my arrival in Mostar, when we met with Mr. Stojic, Bojic, Mr. Coric, and possibly you at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you believe that in October, I was in Mostar. Would that be the conclusion that we can make, that in October 1992, I must have been in Mostar? If that is a possibility, then that possibility could have been in October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my point. I cannot put -- I cannot say it for definite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 60, you claim that Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic was the commander of the HVO Main Staff, and then you go on to say that he had command and control of the entire HVO military organisation together with General Slobodan Praljak. Then, in the next paragraph, paragraph 61, towards the end, you say that the highest military commander of the HVO, General Petkovic, and then in 62, you say General Slobodan Praljak was the HVO commander in chief, and his office was also in the HVO headquarters in West Mostar. So in your statement, we have certain categorical clear cut statements and allegations that is that Brigadier General Petkovic was the commander and that he had an office in Mostar, but here in court you say that you may have seen me in October in Mostar and, yesterday, in the -- in your testimony, you said you had met with me implying several occasions. Could you give a brief commentary? On what grounds do you claim that there were two commanders of the HVO, that I had an office in Mostar, where and when? Or do you still stand by what you said, that you may have met me once in October when I wasn't grey haired but young, dark-haired and charming?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't actually use the word "charming". I did say in my testimony that I saw you rarely, in fact the information with respect to your position within the HVO that you refer to there was information that was given to me by UNPROFOR. My experience in dealing with General Petkovic led me to believe that he was the commander of the HVO on the ground, and that's where the contrast might appear. But to repeat, I said it in my testimony, I had no dealings with you during my period there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please give this map to the witness? And the part marked in red, could it be placed under the ELMO so that everyone can see it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, I will now show you a map of Mostar, in view of the fact that you went there frequently, and we'll try to establish on this map a few matters that you may have known or you may not have known, but we'll see. Let us, to save time, I have marked here, on top, the road going through Eastern Mostar, below the hill. Can you see it? The road going above the River Neretva towards the top of the map. Yes, that's the one. Do you know that that was the main road from Ploce to Sarajevo, Ploce, Capljina, Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, Sarajevo. Or further on Rama, Prozor, Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf, depending on the name given by the different entities. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The circle which I have marked with a number 1, is that the old bridge according to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall stop there just for a moment. In your statement, in paragraph 73, you stated that the army of Republika Srpska targeted you as were you crossing the bridge near the dam, and in paragraph 24, you said that it was very difficult to cross the Old Bridge, it was extremely difficult to cross the bridge and enter the eastern side of Mostar, and there is another statement according to which you crossed along the dam below the bridge that was south of the Old Bridge. Can you please tell us where the dam that was south of the Old Bridge was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seems to be a little bit of confusion. I don't think I actually said I was targeted on the Old Bridge by Serb artillery. I was targeted on the bridge close to the hydroelectric dam which I don't know if we can see it here but down somewhere down here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Is there a dam and bridge south of the Old Bridge? Is there a dam south of the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "dam" might be incorrect. Hydroelectric plant, but there is a bridge down there which you are probably aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: A bridge below the Old Bridge, you're claiming that there was another bridge to the south of the Old Bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But you said that the only communication between East and West Mostar, in the old town, was the Old Bridge. Which bridge was further south than the Old Bridge? Which -- and had not been destroyed? Their Honours have been in the case for a long time. They have seen the pictures. Was there a bridge south of the old bridge that was not destroyed and that could be crossed, whether it was a bridge or a dam or whatever?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a bridge, sir, which was damaged but passable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Tell me also something else. During your tour of duty, did hundreds of people cross the Old Bridge going left and right?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are now talking about the Stari Most bridge; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Will you look at circle number 2, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, what General Praljak has just asked you, whether people crossed the Old Bridge and you said yes, hundreds of people. But what I would like to know, the people who were crossing the bridge that you must have seen because you said yes, do you remember whether they were wearing military uniforms? Did you see military men circulating across that bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the traffic of people across the bridge, Your Honour, from October to my stay in March, decreased significantly, but to answer your direct question, I did not see military -- people wearing military pattern uniform crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, when you were crossing to the left and to the right, that there was a check-point in control of the crossing. Also, do you -- are you aware that this check-point existed on both ends of the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on, please. The circle marked with the number 4, would you agree with me in saying that this is the area known as Vranica, where the 4th Corps headquarters was located of the 41st Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the communication system? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters was located there, sir. I'm in no position to say the communications system was located there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that dozens of officers of the BiH army were working there, either belonging to the 4th Corps or the 41st Army, who went to work there on a daily basis, crossing the bridge, going back home, so that throughout that period, dozens of people were working in that building, officers, security people, communications officers and so on?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that dozens of people were working in that building. In fact on the occasions that I was there I think I said yesterday there were not that many people in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. The circle marked with 2, would you agree with me that that is the Rondo, the location that you have mentioned, number 2, the circle number 2, is that the Rondo to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The circle with the number there is that the hotel Ero that was also mentioned, Mr. Karnavas spoke about it, about the hotel, the restaurant, et cetera, is that the Ero Hotel?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, sir, my memory doesn't go back that far but if you tell me it is, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. If you just say I can't remember, that will make things easier. The numbers H1, H2, H3 and H4, have been written to mark the hospitals on the right-hand of the river. H1 is Bijeli Brijeg, H2 is the surgery department, H3 is the psychiatry ward, and ophthalmology, H4 is the tuberculosis infirmary. Did you ever visit any one of these four hospitals on the west side of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I visited three out of the four, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that throughout that period, these were hospitals as we call them, they had everything a hospital has, beds, hospital beds, for patients, some had labs, some had surgery wards, X-ray equipment and so on? Did you see all this in those hospitals, all the elements that contribute to a hospital being a hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my memory isn't that good on the issue but I do remember in this location here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: H1, yes?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: H1 was a well-equipped hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that throughout your tour of duty and later as well, the entire population of the city of Mostar was treated and the surroundings of course regardless of sex, age, religion or ethnicity? Are you aware of that. If you don't remember, never mind. Tell me so, so that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a conflict with this because I hear what you're saying, sir, but the reality I found on the ground on the eastern side of the river, as I already gave in testimony, was slightly different, so when you ask me am I aware that all people were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, please, please, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is very clear. Please answer my question. Should a discussion be necessary for you to repeat what you have already said, Their Honours will allow to you do so. I have to abide by the instructions I have. Did you notice during your visit that as far as the hospitals I have enumerated are concerned, that there was any kind of discrimination in treatment regarding gender, age, ethnicity, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that treatment was free of charge?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, the previous no, what does that exactly refer to because the question is rather complex. Does it mean you do not know or does it mean certain facts were not as Mr. Praljak puts them to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means I wasn't aware of these different groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, during your testimony, you said that you brought medicines to the war hospital on the east side. You even used the plural, hospitals. My question is a simple one. Tell me or draw for us a single hospital on the east side that had a single bed for a patient or a single X-ray or a single laboratory or surgery or anything that would be reminiscent of a hospital. Just point to a single institution that might be described as a hospital very loosely even?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to ask if we could indicate specifically what period of time this drawing is to pertain to. When -- when -- what's the period of time that he wants the witness to address? What month or period?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Exclusively the period from his arrival until Mr. Lane left. I'm talking about that period. I'm limiting my questions to that period. So I repeat: Could you draw on the east side or point to a single building or location which, in the broadest sense could be called a hospital in which you saw a single patient in a bed or an x-ray apparatus or anything that might look like a hospital. If you could, could you please indicate where that was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the delivery, and it was only one convoy, of the equipment that you refer to was done at speed, as I indicated, and I do not know nor can I remember where we dropped that stuff off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I won't be asking you about that convoy, what you brought, et cetera. I'm asking whether you personally, your feet, your body, your eyes, did you enter any building, any premise in which you saw a bed-ridden patient or anything that might look like a hospital, a laboratory, an x-ray apparatus, on the east side, a surgery theatre, at the time when you personally went there? Did you yourself with your own eyes see such a building?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us where that was roughly?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already indicated that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have an IC number for this map? Will you just move the map a little so we can see north, south, east, west? You will see I've marked that on the map. Do you agree with me that these are the sides of the world? North, south, east, west?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we will agree on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have an IC number if Your Honours believe the witness should sign the map, he can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have a number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document just marked shall be given Exhibit number IC 696. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness sign the map and put a date on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, put down today's date, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 2D 00458 on the e-court, please? 2D 00458. 2D 00458.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Lane, will you please read. The date coincides with the period when you were there, 8th of March, signed by Sulejman Budakovic. Let me ask you first whether you know who Sulejman Budakovic was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that he was deputy commander or rather Chief of Staff of the 4th Corps? He was deputy commander, the deputy of Arif Pasalic, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, we seem not to have this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D 00458. No, it's not in my set of documents, Your Honours. Because I took it from Mr. Stojic's Defence but we have it on the e-court. I unfortunately didn't have time to get a copy. I just wanted to check something. It's not due to any laziness or irresponsibility on my part. It is very difficult for us from the detention to communicate with others. So let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you read the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, there is one of the problems one experiences when the accused conducts a cross-examination -- the cross-examination himself rather than having his attorney do it. Because if his attorney was able to do it or was conducting the cross then we would all have the hard copy and indeed the witness would be in a position to look at the paper in front of him rather than trying to read off the screen which is not the preferable way at all to proceed, I think, in fairness to the witness. So you know, it's -- hopefully it's just one document but if there are more documents that the witness is not provided with on paper we are going to object to it. There is a procedure and it's not being followed. And it's not being followed because the accused is conducting the cross-examination and we shouldn't suffer as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, thank you, Your Honour. I have to be quite sincere that Mr. Praljak asked permission from me to use this document, so I take on the blame if I did not understand his request for a hard copy. As far as I know, it is the only such document. It is brief. It is in the e-court, and I don't think the witness will have difficulty in reading it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, a response on my part. You said that the Prosecution should not suffer. In substance, you are right, but when you look at the document, which I discovered the same time as you, our professional knowledge should allow us to reduce the prejudice. This document is not complicated, and your great professionalism should enable you to deal with all possible questions relating to this document, but basically, you are right, the Defence should give you and us the list of documents and the documents itself, but Mr. Praljak has explained that from the Detention Unit, there is some difficulty in doing that. So please continue, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that it is addressed to the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade and it says, based on the agreement with the HVO on joint engagement of artillery units against the same aggressor, the common aggressor, you should employ a single artillery weapon from your unit, howitzer 122 millimetres, D30, together with support staff and artillery chief. My question is very brief: Are you aware, during your tour of duty, that the army of BiH and the HVO were jointly fighting the army of Republika Srpska? Are you aware of that, that the front lines towards the army of Republika Srpska were jointly manned by the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, sir. But since this document is in front of me, would you -- if I'm permitted to ask you a question in connection to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, sir. It's me asking the questions. I'd be very happy, please don't misunderstand me if Their Honours would give me another hour's time I would be glad to hear any questions from you but unfortunately, because of the clock which is ticking, I have quite a bit more to cover. My second question: Whether you, as a professional soldier, noticed that the BiH army had artillery weapons? Here we see mention of a D30 howitzer. Did you notice that they did have artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that, sir, is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then the last sentence mentions a mixed division. We won't go into discussing how many artillery weapons such a unit has but let us now move on. I'm referring to my set of documents, 3D 01094. 3D 01094.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this in my file?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There are only a couple of documents in this, my set of documents, 3D -- 3D 01094. It's a document dated the 16th of January 1993. It's a lengthy document. There is no signature, but it is the Chief of Staff of the HVO, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. I would like to look through parts of that document with you. So it's dated the 16th of January. It is a collective report regarding the situation and positions of the HVO on the battle front. In the Croatian it is page 2 but you will find it easily. The report from Gornji Vakuf. "Until 1800 hours ... " Have you found it? Not for the night. In the English, it says, "Up until 16 or 1800 hours. Report from Gornji Vakuf." It says that sniper fire continued by the Muslim forces. We have one dead, one wounded soldier, Anto Ljubas wounded and Mato Gazilj from Hrasnica was killed. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But look at the report from Gornji Vakuf 1600 hours and it says, "In relation to the last report, the situation has changed somewhat. The Chetnik shelling has stopped and the canyon fire of Muslim and our forces continued but of lesser intensity." I'm interested in this sentence and I want to ask you, when you were there in October in Uskoplje or Gornji Vakuf and when were you there on the 18th of January, again in Gornji Vakuf, were you personally aware or informed by the British battalion or anyone else that -- that forces of the army of Republika Srpska were regularly shelling Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that there had been shelling by the Serb forces. But I don't think the word "regular" was used.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. We'll leave out the regular part. Have a look at another document, 3D 01095, 3D 01095. It's in the binder. It's a report from the HVO Main Staff dated the 29th of January 1993. It relates to the 28th of January 1993. It concerns that date. As far as I understand, you were in the area at the time. It says report from Prozor. It's the first page, in the Croatian text, report from Prozor. "The cease-fire is mostly respected in the conflict areas between the BH army and our forces. In the villages with Muslim inhabitants, sporadic firing from infantry weapons can be heard. The BH army forces have been fortifying in the temporarily occupied areas. Negotiations on prison exchanges ongoing." At the time, had the cease-fire already been implemented and was the fighting gradually calming down? Does your information, does your knowledge, tally with what you can see in this document?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Have a look at item 3, please. The southeastern operative zone, the southeastern operative zone of Herzegovina report from Mostar at 1900 hours. I don't want to read this out aloud but could you read it to yourself, to the end of the document, where it says the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO Milivoj Petkovic, they talk about artillery firing, Chetniks used large calibre weapons, then it says 40 shells on Blagaj 5, then it says the same number were fired on Drvenik, Rotimlje, and then the centre of Potoci, the right bank of the Neretva River, anti-aircraft artillery, shell to the Mostar hydroelectric plant, and then there is a report from Mostar, the 29th of January, and it says, in Bijelo Polje and Podvelezje, Vucja Glava, there were shells, Chetniks hit, fired on Drvenik, Blagaj, Plohovice [phoen] it says, Rotimlje and Treban [phoen] were subjected to artillery fire and approximately 100 shells fell on this area.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, sir, what paragraph are you reading from there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The third paragraph, the operative zone of Southeastern Herzegovina, report from Mostar. It's the penultimate page in the Croatian version that's probably the case in the English version too, I'll try and find it, item 3, the penultimate page in the English version, Southeastern Herzegovina report from Mostar. At 1900 hours. It's the third page in the English version. And to the end of the page. It's very simple. My question is as follows, sir: While you were down in the area, and in Mostar, et cetera, did you hear from ABiH or HVO commanders or did you personally see that the Republika Srpska artillery from Konjic and to the south to Stolac regularly shelled the front lines inhabited settlements, Mostar, both the eastern and western part of Mostar, probably because of the battlefield which was close to Eastern Mostar was subjected to more intense shelling but were you familiar with the regular shelling of the Republika Srpska army during your stay in the area?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I referred to it yesterday in my testimony and I said I experienced it on the road to Stolac on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Here is another document 3D 01096, the 3rd of March 1993. It's the following document in my binder, the 3rd of March, it's a report of a similar kind. Have a look at item 3, the operative zone of Southeastern Herzegovina. We'll go through it rapidly. At 1500 hours, two tank shells were fired on Hum at 1545 the Chetniks opened fire on a convoy that was under UNPROFOR's court. While I was crossing the HC bridge, they used 40 millimetre cannon and UNPROFOR responded to the Chetnik fire and opened fire on them and so on and so forth. You told me that you were also shelled. Can you confirm my hypothesis that the Serbian artillery regularly shelled the Mostar area, the eastern and western part of Mostar, the eastern a little more and to the south and north of Mostar as well; is that correct? Was that the case while you were down there in the area?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yes, what you've said is absolutely right and you did also say that there was obviously more shelling in East Mostar than West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could the usher please place another map on the ELMO? We will now be dealing with Stolac. It's a small map of a wider area. Have a look at it, sir, and while you're looking at the map I'll just put a few questions to you. The Kostana hospital that you visited regularly, do you know that the patients in that hospital or most of the patients had been there prior to the beginning of the conflict? These were patients who were very ill, they had very severe bone diseases. Were you aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, sir. I was also aware that it was actually a refuge centre also in addition to being a hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know that the wounded who were treated by Dr. Kapic were most frequently sent on in the direction of Split and Metkovic and patients with bone diseases remained there so the wounded who were supposed to be operated on went towards Split and Metkovic? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's partially correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that Metkovic and Split are in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the hospital in Metkovic was a military hospital that belonged to the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually visited it in my time there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that all those wounded, all the patients in the Kostana hospital up until the end of February 1992, were taken out of that hospital, taken away from the hospital -- sir, up until the end of February 1993, do you know that all the hospitals from the Kostana hospital were taken to the Republic of Croatia? Do you know that towards the end of February, there were no longer any patients with a severe bone diseases in that hospital? They were all taken to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people in that hospital post-February 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, look, I'm not saying that wasn't the case, but the first group of the wounded [indiscernible] was constantly being shelled and ABiH soldiers and Croatian soldiers were there but after, in March 1993, did you see a single patient with a bone disease? I'm not referring to the wounded who had gone to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I object to the question. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what's the relevance of this question? What are you trying to establish, to prove?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I want to demonstrate that after February 1993, it became a military hospital for the first echelon, as they say, for the wounded, for the civilians and for the soldiers, and then secondly I want to show that the Republic of Croatia and HVO doctors found the resources to move these patients who were immobile. They had been transported to Croatia and they were taken care of there. So the relevance of the question is that the leadership of the Republic of Croatia and that includes us, who have been accused of a joint criminal enterprise, well that would mean that these patients over which there were 100 would have been left there, which is what the Serbs did when they were there. So my question is relevant. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may I apologise to General Praljak, since my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, was absent maybe I could say why this is relevant. In the course of the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution put a series of questions to the witness about the Kostana hospital. The witness mentioned the difficult situation in the hospital, he mentioned the fact that there was no electricity or water. And the situation was described as if the HVO was responsible for that situation. It was as if the HVO had prevented food and medicine from being provided, and other necessities for the hospital. So I think it's very important to clarify how in fact this hospital functioned. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Praljak has explained what he believed the situation was like in the hospital, invalids had been sent to Croatia and in February this hospital had been transformed into a military or wartime hospital. What do you say about this? Is that true, false, you don't know, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree with that assessment, Your Honour. That's not the picture that I found on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you tell me when did you visit the hospital in March, either you yourself or someone from your team in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I left the mission area in the 22nd of March and I cannot be definite about the date but I would have visited that hospital within one week of leaving on the -- seven to 10 days before I left on the 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now for my next question. Have a look at the map that you have. I've marked it. Let's try and establish some facts first of all. Do you agree that under number 1 you can see Stolac; number 2 Mostar; number 3, Siroki Brijeg; number 4, Posusje; number 5, Jablanica; number 7 Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf -- no I apologise, Rama; 8, Gornji Vakuf; 9, Bugojno; 6, Konjic; and H1, marks the Kostana hospital; H2 -- no, H2 is the hospital in Domanovici. So, have these places that I have mentioned been correctly marked on this map?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in Domanovici, marked with the letter D, was a fairly large hospital for patients with a serious mental illnesses, schizophrenia, et cetera? Do you know there was a very big hospital of that kind at that location?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that at the beginning of your arrival, thanks to Dr. Sandrk, Gveric, many of those patients had been transferred from that hospital and thanks to humanitarian organisations from Italy, most of them were provided with accommodation there? Do you know that all these patients were moved and placed in good institutions, partly in Croatia, but mostly in Italy? And in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of what patients, sir, are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm referring to the patients from Domanovici, the patients who were in that hospital that had been there nor a long time, they were patients from the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had incurable mental illnesses, paranoia, schizophrenia, these people were quite incapable of taking care of themselves, and these people were people who belonged to various nations, they were people of various religious faiths, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If you take the marker, could you trace the route you used to go to Gornji Vakuf and to Uskoplje, Mostar, Jablanica, Rama, Uskoplje, can you show me the route? Could you use a marker of some kind?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Obviously, you used two routes towards Jablanica and further up and then you used the other route through the Vran mountain. Did you know that this route was called the route of salvation?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have one more question. Do you know that the Republic of Croatia at the time that you were in the area provided hospitals in Mostar with surgical teams, orthopaedists, surgeons for internal bleeding, et cetera, they often went there to provide assistance because there were a lot of wounded, they went to Mostar from Croatia, had you experienced such a thing there? Did you meet those people?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Since you have said that you've been a professional soldier for 32 years, could you use this map to trace approximately the positions of the Republika Srpska army in Stolac and towards Mostar and to the north towards Konjic and could you show where the HVO positions and where the ABiH positions were, if you can, do so, if not, say so and we'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please sign the map?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document marked by the witness will be given Exhibit number IC 697. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we place this map on the Elmo, too and it would be good if we could see this part that has been marked, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll now deal with the Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf area. I have a map here and I have marked certain things of importance on the map. In the course of your examination-in-chief, you said that in December 1992 -- correction in November, you visited Uskoplje and Gornji Vakuf and you went through the Jablanica-Uskoplje route and you said that at the time the artillery in Makljen was facing Prozor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said on that occasion that you saw from Makljen, that you saw Gornji Vakuf from Makljen and you saw the artillery shelling there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I actually said was that I went to some key terrain to get a view of Gornji Vakuf in the distance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, I've marked some elevations here, from Makljen towards Gornji Vakuf, from Makljen to Gornji Vakuf. I've encircled these elevations and I want to show you the following. The height of these elevations, as they continue towards Gornji Vakuf, elevation 13 is 1176 metres; 14, 1114 metres; Elevation 12 - we are going in towards Vakuf - 1094 metres; elevation 10, 1261 metres; 11, 1228 metres, it's higher than the other ones; elevation 8, 1072; 9, 1197 metres; elevation 7, 1121 metres; elevation 6, 1007 metres; elevation 5, 1025 metres; elevation 4, Mackovac, 991 metres; elevation 1, 876 metres; and the elevation above the town of Vakuf itself, above the repeater, is 785 metres. In Vakuf, marked with number 3, 654 metres. Vakuf is at a height of 654 metres. And elevation 2 is 785 metres. It's just above the previous one. Sir, do you see this road towards Vakuf and does it go through the valley between the mountains? Does this route go through the valley? So when you used this road to go from Makljen to Uskoplje to the left or the right of you was anything visible apart from the forests? I think even the Judges have taken that route. But have a look at the map. What I'm telling you is that correct, when you take this route to Vakuf, is it correct to say that there is nothing you can see apart from the forest to the left and to the right of the road? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will be aware, as I explained to you, the majority of times I drove into Gornji Vakuf was in the back of a Warrior armoured car.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Sir, please, whether you say I was at the rear, I didn't have binoculars, I was sleeping, et cetera, well, this is all taking up my time and it's of no use to us. When you went down that road, did you see anything to the left or the right, yes, no, I can't remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, the comment about I was sleeping? That wasn't said by the witness. And it's insulting to suggest that the witness was sleeping in the back of an APC when he was heading up to Gornji Vakuf to carry out his mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think any insult was meant, it was figurative, like the classical reason why one if not seeing what one should see, while travelling. I mean, if that is insulting we must be very, very careful because that's the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, we have a map, and various elevations have been marked on the map, and we see that Gornji Vakuf is at an altitude of 600 or 700 metres and the point of departure from Makljen, which is where you were is further up, is higher up. But General Praljak says that when you look at all these elevations that have been numbered, well, he says that all these elevations are at an altitude of over a thousand metres. Now we are dealing with a very military issue. He says from the position where you were supposed to be, it's impossible to see Gornji Vakuf. That's his thesis. I wasn't there. Unless it's necessary for the Chamber to go there to see this for themselves. So what do you have to tell us? Are you sure of what you are saying or do you have any doubts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm 100 per cent positive in what I'm saying and I also said in the testimony the other day that I only saw a small part of Gornji Vakuf. I didn't say I saw the whole town of Gornji Vakuf. I said I had to find some key ground to -- and I did, locate it, so I could see a part of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Praljak, what I do not understand about your question, whether from the road one can see anything, because the witness has never spoken of something he has seen from the road but upon a question he has expressly said that at one point, the car stopped and he walked to a place from where he could see something. So what is the interest of knowing whether he saw something from a place where he never pretended that he saw something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct. I first wanted to establish what one could see from the road, and my assumption is that from the road and right up until the entrance to Gornji Vakuf it's not possible to see anything. That was my first question. That's what I wanted to clarify. And the second question concerned what Judge Antonetti said, elevations from Makljen up to the one above Vakuf, at a higher altitude than Makljen itself, elevation 11 and 7, for example, so when you take the route -- road, you can't see anything, when you set off from Gornji Vakuf, right up until elevation 1 where you can -- from where you can see the left part of Vakuf and it's only from elevation 2 right above Vakuf that you can see the town in the valley. It's possible to see from elevation 1 Bistrica, et cetera, but you can't see Vakuf itself. Anyone who knows anything about maps can see this especially since there is a forest there. So you can't see anything from any of the elevations apart from the ones I have mentioned, you can't see anything from the road either and that's what I'm claiming. I'm trying to establish what could be seen without binoculars, to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me, do you have a rough recollection of the position from which it was possible for you to see something?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already said in my previous testimony I stopped at a number of locations and eventually found an area that I could observe Gornji Vakuf but also remember that I also said there was shelling going on so I wasn't hanging around the area but I saw Gornji Vakuf as I said, a part of it, sufficient to see shelling and leave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, you have now point X and point Y on the map. What is the distance with this scale on the map between X and Y? The scale is one to 50.000. How many kilometres is equivalent to one centimetre on this map when the scale is one to 50.000?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think are we talking about 25 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, sir. One centimetre on the map, how many metres is equivalent to one centimetre on the map, given the scale of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to lend him your ruler.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If he wants it. [Speakers overlapping]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, let us first find out what is the equivalent of one centimetre? I too have a ruler. One centimetre on the map is equal to how many kilometres in reality? If the scale is one to 50.000.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One centimetre equals 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we have 21 centimetres, you can check if you like and that is equal to ten and a half kilometres. You said that you didn't have binoculars, that you saw shelling, so I won't dwell on the point any further. What we have heard we have heard. One further point, did you see the shelling in November 1992 or on the 18th of January, when you were in an UNPROFOR armoured vehicle going to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said I saw shelling in November.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. On this map, I have also drawn A and B. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know where the road marked with a B leads to?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume it goes to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: True. What about the road marked with an A? Do you know where it goes?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never -- I was never on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. My question regarding these two roads has been prompted by your statement that Gornji Vakuf at the time of the conflict was an isolated town, that the Muslims were isolated towards the north. Since you never took road A, my next question would be as follows: Can you draw on this map at the time you were there where the positions of the ABiH were and where were the positions of the HVO at the time of the conflict, when you were touring the area, could you roughly indicate where the positions of the two parties were? It was a long time ago. If you can't, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you show us in what direction were the front lines which were jointly held before by the HVO and the ABiH towards the Serbs or rather where were the front lines with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you show us on this map the separation lines within the town of Vakuf itself? Which part of the town of Vakuf, during the conflict, were held -- was held by the ABiH and what part by the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot show you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went there, did you ask yourself why the conflict had broken out between the ABiH and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf? What was the reason for this limited conflict?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already said in testimony that my priority in Gornji Vakuf was to ensure a cease-fire was brought into effect and held. The reasons for the conflict at that stage did not concern me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, we are turning around a little bit in circles. General Praljak is asking you what were the reasons for the conflicts between the ABiH and the hover in Gornji Vakuf. Your answer is that your concern was to make the cease-fire effective. That's fine. But whether one is a military man, one must ask oneself why the conflict had broken out in the first place. So that is the question that has been put to you. Even though you were focusing on the cease-fire, did you try to find out why the conflict had broken out, who started it, and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my opinion that this conflicts was started by the HVO and when we went, as I think I've mentioned in the -- my previous testimony, when we sat down to negotiate a cease-fire, the Armija, Muslim side, were extremely anxious to obtain a cease-fire and the HVO on the other side most definitely were not. So I think that would point to where the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not quite sure that the record is correct. I'm afraid that I don't understand whether this was the witness's opinion or whether it was a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that your opinion or is it a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my professional military opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then probably additional question to that would be appropriate. Sir, have you found out any facts on base which you confirm that of concrete, direct facts, or is this just general observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to cross-examination by tag team is what we would call it where I come from. This cross-examination is being conducted by the accused and I'm opposed to the passing of the witness back and forth between the accused and his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought we were here to gets to the truth. Why is the Prosecution always afraid of the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not afraid of the truth, Mr. President. It's the procedure. I raised procedure earlier, and yes, we are all professionals and we can handle one document but it's the procedure and I'm concerned about the procedure being altered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, regarding procedure, you're right. But if the Defence were to implement the procedure very strictly, what would happen? There would be Mr. Kovacic, who would write down on a piece of paper a message to Mr. Praljak to ask him to put a certain question. So that would be a waste of time because as Mr. Karnavas has said so well, we are here to find the truth. Let us try and do so. It is already five to 4.00, unfortunately time flies and we have to have a break now. Normally, Mr. Praljak, my understanding is that your time has run out. How much more time do you need? How many more questions do you have? Five minutes? You're showing us seven fingers, so seven fingers so we will resume in 20 minutes and you'll have seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Before giving the floor to Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stringer, do you have any news about our witness for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I looked for Mr. Scott and couldn't find him. He might be running around trying to find a witness for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we need to know that very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We are attempting to communicate by e-mail as well during the course of the proceedings. And if I'm -- we will obviously inform the Trial Chamber and the parties as soon as we have something firm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's not forget the last map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, if we may cover a couple of questions quickly. While you were in Gornji Vakuf and working on the implementation of the signed cease-fire, was the basic problem raised by the HVO to cover up the trenches that the BiH army had dug at all the elevations around Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said in testimony that the problem I had was Colonel Siljeg's absence from the signing ceremony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, will you please listen to my question? According to what I know, the HVO had two basic demands for the implementation of the cease-fire, and those were to fill in the trenches which the army had done on the elevations around Gornji Vakuf, and the departure of the Jajce Brigade from Gornji Vakuf. Do you remember that those were the preconditions set by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not the main preconditions set by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me the following. The names Abdulah Topcic, Fahrudin Agic and Prijic Hanefija known as Paraga, do these names ring a bell at all? Have you heard of those names?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes, sir, yes, two of them, two of them, two of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you heard what Prijic Hanefija, the commander of the military police of the BiH army, did in Gornji Vakuf? Do you know what his position was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please sign the map now and can I have an IC number for this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour the map just signed by the witness shall be given Exhibit number IC 698. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to correct the record because there may be difficulties later, on page 42, line 12, it says the departure of identities, the question was the departure of the Jajce Brigade, [In English] Meaning brigade from Jajac -- from Jajce, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Let me show you one more map, please. There are copies for Their Honours, too. And a map for the witness. Until the map is distributed, may I ask you something? One more thing about Posusje and that will bring to an end my cross-examination. As you travelled along Herceg-Bosna, did you see a single factory -- you have the map behind you that's the map -- did you see in the area a single factory that was operating or producing anything at all, spare parts, or manufacturing anything? Did you see an oil refinery, a medicines factory, while you were there, during your tour of duty, did you see anything functioning, a factory?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't honestly answer whether I saw a factory functioning, but I saw normal life functioning in restaurants and places like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So look at this map. It is a map of Herzegovina. So that we can see the various elevations on it. I have marked Posusje on it, the road of salvation, and is this one of the routes that you used to reach Gornji Vakuf? Rama is also marked.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please use a marker to mark the route from Ploce, Capljina, Mostar, Jablanica, this road that you, among others, took to reach Gornji Vakuf, could you mark it? My question is did this route go along the Neretva River valley? It goes along the river valley, Metkovic, Capljina, Mostar, Jablanica and then to the left.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It goes along the river valley, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was this the main road passing through East Mostar used by the UNHCR convoys to carry supplies from the port of Ploce up to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Posusje and what you saw in Posusje, do you know that in 1992 after the attack that is a little before your arrival and during your stay through this refugee centre, more than 100.000 refugees passed through this centre, some staying for shorter periods, others for longer periods, before they travelled on to the Republic of Croatia? Are you aware of that? That more than 100.000 refugees using the road of salvation first of all a large number of Muslims afterwards both Croats and Muslims, they passed through this centre all ethnicities, that is Muslims and Croats, before they were taken in by the Republic of Croatia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into Posusje?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And sorry, when? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In a period starting from April 1992 and it went on until you left the area. So in the period from April 1992 until March 1993, that using this road of salvation, more than 100.000 people came to Posusje, stayed there for a while, both Bosniaks and Croats, before going on to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be my experience.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you didn't talk to the person who was in charge of this refugee centre or camp? You don't know his name and you never spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually did speak to the relevant authorities in the camp on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When Jajce was occupied or captured by the army of Republika Srpska, do you know how many Croats took this route? You were already there then. And reached the refugee centre in Posusje? How many Croats from Jajce passed through this refugee centre? Are you aware of the figure?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the word Posusje, the etymology of the word, means something dry, dried, without water? In other words, that in this town, until 1995, there was a very small water supply system and that in 1992 and in 1993, water had to be brought there mostly by tanks? Cisterns, water tanks?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very clear in what I said about Posusje yesterday. I targeted humanitarian aid where it was and how it could be brought to Posusje and I failed to get that agreed with certain people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, your task was to observe and to care about humanitarian aid and there were tens and thousands of people who passed through there, as you said yesterday. I'm asking do you know that at the time Posusje was a town without water and that water had to be brought there in water tanks, in 1992 and during your tour of duty? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you're telling me that's the truth, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interject at this point because I sense some tension here. General Praljak is asking a very legitimate question because the assertion by the gentleman based on his observation was whether there were some omissions or failures on the part of certain people to take care of certain other people. Now, the question is very legitimate. It calls for a yes or no. Either he knew or he doesn't know. First he tells us what his mission was. Which he's told us on direct, he told us on cross, he's told us a hundred times; we know it. Now he's just eating up time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel, I have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me finish my submission and you can say what you want. He was asked concretely he had to be asked a second time. I would ask the Trial Chamber to direct the witness to be forthright and forthcoming with General Praljak and anyone else who asks a question. He can certainly say directly what the answer is and then if he wishes to explain, other than tell us what he's already told us a hundred times, you know, I think you need to instruct the witness, Mr. President. It's getting tiresome sitting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, you should answer the question when the question requires a yes, no, I don't know, answer, if there is a question that requires a comment on your part, you should then provide that additional information. Mr. Praljak, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it's necessary to conclude now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just have another two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you answer my question? Do you know, did you know that Posusje means a place without water? If you look at the word's etymology, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sir, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that in 1992 and 1993 water tanks had to be used to deliver water to Posusje and that was the case right up until 1995, but we're not interested in that. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware there was a shortage of water, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know what the population of Posusje was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And I have one last question to put to you: If I told you by paraphrasing a book by Kundera, the title of which is "the Unbearable Lightness of Being", that you not just you but because of the unbearable lightness of drawing conclusions contributed to the state of confusion? You did not realise how much energy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is this a question? I think you are giving moral evaluation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge Trechsel, I'm just asking the witness a question given the overall situation at the time the witness was in the area, given the number of inhabitants, the water problems, et cetera, was the witness aware at that time of the way in which one had to organise everything for 100.000 refugees? This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many problems there were? Do you know how many resources had been allocated for the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question directly, do I know, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that because of the fact that there were refugees in-- do you know that because of the fact that refugees were in Posusje, school hadn't started, not just in Posusje but in other villages too because refugees were all over the place, this is my last question but were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm not opposed to General Praljak having additional time. At this stage, I can tell the Trial Chamber that I would like to reserve 30 minutes for redirect and that, you know, beyond that the Trial Chamber as between General Praljak and Ms. Alaburic can allocate the time as it sees fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please answer the question about the start of the school time period in Posusje. Can you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Lane for answering my questions. Thank you, Your Honours for granting me additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've provided us with two maps. If you could give us two other maps that would be very useful, because this map is very revealing. We can locate the towns, the villages, the routes, the villages and the forests of Herzegovina. So it would be very useful if you could provide us with two additional maps so that each judge could have a -- one map. That's the Chamber's request. And perhaps Mr. Stringer would appreciate a map too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We would like the map also, Mr. President. We would like to have a copy if that could be arranged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have another one here for you. I'll bring a second one. And I'll provide the Prosecutor with a copy of the map too. I haven't brought additional ones with me.
