utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll give this one to Mr. Stringer since the Judges already have two, and you will bring an additional one. Very well. Would you like an IC number for this? Mr. Praljak and a signature too, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the document just marked by the witness shall be given IC number 699. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order not to establish a precedent we usually receive an electronic version of a map from the Prosecution. The Prosecution will get an electronic version of the map for when the Registry has scanned it. It's not my responsibility for printing them out. We had difficulty in obtaining these. But this is Mr. Praljak's goodwill to provide the Prosecution and the judges with these copies but I wouldn't like to establish a precedent here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that I'm providing you with. We have a slight disagreement, my counsel and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor for an hour now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, dear colleagues, good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. My name is Vesna Alaburic, I'm a lawyer from Zagreb and I'm defending General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings. I'd like to spend the first ten minutes clarifying certain details that relate to the EC mission because I believe that there are certain discrepancies between your testimony and the testimony of your colleague, Christopher Beese, and we examined your colleague for a five-day period. First of all, allow me to summarise what I believe was relevant in your testimony. With regard to the refugees in Posusje, you told us that you didn't know who they were, where they were from, why they had taken refuge, you said that you were only concerned about how to help them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually said I did know who they were. You're right, I didn't know where they came from, and you're right, my objective was to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I understood your testimony differently. I thought you had said you didn't even know who they were. Can you tell us which towns these refugees had come from?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, what I meant was I thought I said that the people were from Muslim background. I don't know what town they came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you see both Croatian and Muslim refugees in Posusje or did you only visit Muslim refugees there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I saw at the time were Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who told you that they were Muslims alone?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through my own eyes having walked through the building itself, and spoken to the administrators of Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't have to time to go into that but usually we don't believe that it's possible to determine whether someone is a Muslim a Croat or a Serb in that area just by seeing them. We believe that other criteria have to be used but let's move on to another subject. In the course of your examination-in-chief, and when answering a question put to you by Mr. Karnavas, you said that you weren't familiar with the organisation of the leadership of the government in Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also said that you weren't familiar with the contents of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And today you told us that you weren't interested in the reasons for the conflict in Gornji Vakuf. You were only interested in the implementation of the cease-fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'll tell you what your colleague, Christopher Beese, said about the same things more or less and for the sake of the transcript, I'll refer to the pages of the transcript where Mr. Beese's testimony can be found. He said that the task of the European monitors was first of all to monitor the events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, secondly to report on those events, and thirdly, to analyse the events, in order to gain a better understanding of the situation and in order to be able to reach good decisions on the conflict. And the reports and the analysis of the European monitors were forwarded to, first of all, the Presidency of the European Community, and secondly, to the ministers of foreign affairs of the member states of the European Community, thirdly, to the ministers of foreign affairs of members of the OSS, because the European monitors cooperated with that organisation. And fourthly, to those involved in peace negotiations in Geneva, initially Vance and Owen and subsequently to Mr. Stoltenberg. The pages of the transcript, 3058. This is where this testimony can be found. 3062, and 3063. Mr. Lane, could you confirm the testimony of your colleague, Mr. Beese? Was that actually the EC mission or in your opinion was the mission of a different nature?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There is nothing in that that I would disagree with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as humanitarian aid is concerned, he said that the only task of the European monitors was to monitor the convoys and the passage of humanitarian aid. This is on page 3070 of the transcript. And he said that obtaining and distributing humanitarian aid was the responsibility of other organisations, for example, the UNHCR, the Red Cross, the Merhamet charity, Caritas and so on and so forth. Would you agree with this testimony given by Mr. Beese as well?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He also told us that the European monitors in the area of the former Yugoslavia played a significant role when it came to implementing the Vance-Owen peace plan and he said that in that regard, they had a twofold task, to interpret the plan for the benefit of the local authorities in the field, to enable them to have a better understanding of the plan, and secondly to give instructions to the local authorities as to what they should do in order to prepare for the implementation of the Vance-Owen peace plan. This testimony can be found on pages 3237 and pages 3238 of the transcript. Mr. Lane, would you also agree with this claim made by Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Beese took over control of Grude on the 23rd of March, when I left the mission area, and that was his focus, that was his mission at that stage. Yes, I would agree with that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I can just clarify what Mr. Beese said, what he said also related to January and February because he was also referring to the events in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. And in February, and the following months. Could we agree that this claim with regard to the Vance-Owen plan concerns the obligation of the European monitors in 1993 in January and February 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was involved deeply, as you're aware, in the cease-fire arrangements and subsequent events in Gornji Vakuf. The Vance-Owen Plan was, as I said at the time, being dealt with by Mr. Bousseau and Mr. Beese, by the way, who arrived later in the area stayed in Siroki Brijeg and dealt directly with Mr. Bousseau.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, I'd now like to present you with a conclusion. Please listen to me carefully. Given what I know and in the light of the testimony of other witnesses, in order to carry out the tasks that the European monitors had, it was necessary to have the following. Well, they had to have knowledge of how the government functioned in various areas, they had to know what the rules of the systems were in various areas of the former Yugoslavia, they had to know about events by obtaining information from various sources, and they also had to have information from the parties in the conflict, fourthly they had to be familiar with the Vance-Owen peace plan and they had to be familiar with the positions of the parties to the conflict with regard to the aforementioned peace plan and fifthly they had to be familiar with the political objectives of the parties in the conflict. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my functions and mission area, I do not agree with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: These five elements have been enumerated very clearly. Could you tell me whether you disagree with all of them or do you agree with some of these claims?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I obviously don't disagree with all, but I do not agree with some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please, could you tell me which claims you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not necessary at various times in my service to know all the parties in the conflict, to be familiar with the Vance-Owen plan, at the time I was there now I'm talking about, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that as of January 1993, you, as a European monitor, should have been familiar with the contents of the Vance-Owen Plan and you should have been familiar with the positions of the parties to the conflict with regard to that plan? You should have known whether someone had signed it, whether someone had objected to it, why they had objected to it?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you at all on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, very well. We can move on. Mr. Lane, given that you are a professional soldier who has been involved in missions in other countries, could you tell me the following? In the missions you were involved in in the Near East or in Afghanistan, was it possible for you to cross the front lines in your vehicle without hindrance? Could you visit various features or military units or was it not possible for you to do this in an absolutely free manner?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question is so huge that there is just no way I can give an answer. How can I compare the war in the Middle East with Afghanistan? How can one compare? They are completely different wars. I mean the question itself doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in an area, in a conflict area, in which the movement of vehicles and monitors wasn't subject to a certain amount of control?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is I have been in areas where they were not subject to control, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when and where?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 1988, 1994, in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And nowhere else and never again?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually not quite true. In Afghanistan, I was in a number of areas where also there was no control, where you could move freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We are talking about conflict areas. Not about areas in which there weren't any conflicts raging.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me be very clear here. I travelled freely in areas where there was conflict in both Lebanon and Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, tell me whether you distinguish between the idea of restriction of movement and control over movement?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you make a distinction between these two concepts? Do you make a distinction between movement that is restricted and that means that you are prohibited from having access to certain zones, do you distinguish this from the control of movement, which involves certain formalities, obtaining certain permits, establishing check-points, but by passing through those check-points or by obtaining the necessary documents it's possible for you to visit the territory that you want to visit. So do you make a distinction between these two concepts?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to answer your question the way you have it -- the way --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell me whether you make a distinction between these two concepts or not?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a distinction obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the time that you were in the area, did the HVO ever say that you couldn't have access to certain features or certain areas? Did they forbid you to go there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when and where?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when but again on the road to Stolac on a number of occasions we were turned back from a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the time that you wanted to pass through the check-points, was there any shelling in the area, was there any ongoing combat?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- we were turned back for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you try to go to the same area after several days?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The normal procedure would be to go to --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about procedure. I'm asking you that if you were sent back from a check-point on one day, did you try to go to the same area several days later? Did you try to pass through those very same check-points several days later, did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having consulted with HVO, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you did go to the areas that you wanted to go to after all, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not when we wanted to go, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But probably when there was no ongoing combat and when it was possible for you to be provided with the highest level of security, could we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, we could not agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We don't have time to go into that, unfortunately. I would now like to clarify something about your first meeting with the leadership of the ABiH in Mostar. I think there are several contradictions and certain things are not clear in this testimony. I think that you said that you spent about a week and a half in Mostar and then you crossed over the bridge on foot to reach Eastern Mostar and you said that upon arrival in Siroki Brijeg after about a week, you came to Eastern Mostar. So could you please tell us when did you exactly go to Eastern Mostar for the first time and meet the commanders of the ABiH there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think what I said was I thought it might be within a week and a half. I also pointed out I wasn't sure. Unfortunately that's not clear in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A week and a half in relation to what? From the time that you arrived in Siroki Brijeg or in relation to the time when you first arrived in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered it. I can't remember, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. But I'm just wondering did Mr. Beese make a mistake from when the day he arrived in the mission area? I don't know what date he arrived in the mission area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has said that it's a confidential document, and I would therefore request that we move into private session. And do whatever is necessary to do with regard to the transmission. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's move into private session and you need to prepare an order for redaction, redact the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Has this refreshed your memory, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel. Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My memory is as is, there is no change, but just what date in 1992 was that written, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This statement was written, I'll tell you, in 2001.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry, sorry, just for my memory, at the beginning of the statement you made there, you spoke about this witness from 1992, can you just tell me when in 1992, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was during the conflict with the Serbs. During the conflict against the Serbs. You were a European monitor, you know that this was the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. And even the period after you left, because the first next date that the witness mentions is May 1993. I would now like to pass on to another topic and that is January 1993, but before we reach Gornji Vakuf, could my set of documents, which is the orange colour set of documents, that you have in front of you, look at document 4D 00394. It's a document that has already been admitted into evidence, an observation for Your Honours, the orange stickers mark the documents that have already been admitted. Witness, because of the shortage of time, we will reduce our conversation about this document so please look at the second paragraph from the bottom. The second paragraph from the bottom, it is dated the 6th of January 1993, whereby the commander of the 4th Corps of the ABiH orders measures to be taken to combat alert because the peace conference in Geneva is under way where we see in the first line, and in the one-but-last paragraph it says that: "Taking into consideration our experience when the aggressor is concerned, it is to be expected that the aggressor forces shall continue particularly during the continuation of the negotiations to launch fierce attacks on the territory to achieve some military victories and territory gains and their units will certainly continue with the attacks on well-known points of Gradacac, Brcko, Tesanj and particularly Sarajevo and east Bosnia." We see from the whole document that the aggressor implies the Serb side. Mr. Lane, were you aware that the BiH army at the beginning of January 1993, because of the peace negotiations in Geneva, is taking measures to raise the level of combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that they were raising the level of combat awareness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. In the course of the examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor showed you a document signed by my client. It is in my set of documents as well, so you can look at it. It is P 1238. The order dated the 20th of January 1993. Signed by Milivoj Petkovic and Arif Pasalic and it has to do with the cessation of hostilities. This is a document we have already seen. My question will relate to a document that preceded this one, so please look at document P --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I can but I won't be asking you about that document. P 01238. 1238.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to be able to find it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It is in the Prosecutor's set of documents but you won't need it. Look at document P 1211. It's a document from the day before, the 19th of January 1993, the president of HZ HB, Mate Boban, the head of the Defence department, addressed to the head of the Defence department and the chief of the Main Staff issues an order banning offensive operations. Have you found the document, Mr. Lane?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have, yeah, it's P 01211, is it.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we see the second page of the English text, please, on the e-court? Tell me, please, Mr. Lane, did you know that Mr. Mate Boban issued this order on the 19th of January and that a decision on a cease-fire was passed by the highest body of the both civilian and military authorities in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Will you look at point 4 of this order, which says that the BH army should be requested to order their troops to stop any further offensive operations against HVO units in view of the fact that the order on the cessation of operations was adopted the next day, it would be logical to assume that the command of the ABiH did order its units to cease fire. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, can we conclude from this specific cease-fire that a cease-fire as a rule ensued after the relevant political decision to that effect was made? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cease-fire, yes, come into operation as we've already discussed in previous testimony for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question is whether we can infer from these documents that a cease-fire would be implemented after the relevant political bodies made the decision to halt fire?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, we could infer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this connection, your colleague, Christopher Beese said that the task of General Petkovic was to implement the decision on a cease-fire and this is in transcript page 3213. Would you agree with that conclusion of your colleague, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then, as you told us, on the 21st of January, there was a truce and you told us that on the 22nd of January, several hours after the truce came into effect, the HVO violated the truce. Is my interpretation correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, though you were not aware of the details of the peace talks in Geneva, did you know that at the beginning of January, a peace conference was being held in Geneva and also towards the end of January, from the 23rd until the 28th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know that General Petkovic was one of the persons participating in the work of the peace conference in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then probably you couldn't know that on the 22nd of January General Petkovic was travelling to Geneva so as to take part at the conference on the 23rd, but did you know at least that he wasn't in the area of Herceg-Bosna on the 22nd of January?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as I pointed out before, I was dealing with Colonel Siljeg. I was not aware that General Petkovic was out of the area, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. My colleague, Mr. Karnavas, showed us yesterday an order by my client, General Petkovic, issued in Geneva on the 24th of January 1993. I will show you that same document now. It was probably by computer. P 1286 is the document. It hasn't been admitted into evidence. 1286. I see you found it. We see now that it is a document dated the 24th of January 1993. Tell us, please, Mr. Lane, did you perhaps on any occasion find out how come that on the 24th of January, this order should be sent from Geneva?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, ma'am, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you aware or did you find out later what was going on in Geneva that would explain why General Petkovic was sending such an order from Geneva? If you didn't know, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question directly, as I've said I was on the ground in Gornji Vakuf so I was not aware of what you're saying here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, Mr. Lane, as a professional soldier, when you read this order, and when you see the word "immediately," written in capitals, with spacing in between, whereby obviously the idea is to emphasise the word, what would your conclusion be as a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cease immediately, stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, the question of a purely military technical nature. This document mentions an advanced forward command post in Prozor. You who were on the ground, what is a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forward command post, sir, is where the officer in charge of the operation would set up his -- one of his headquarters so he can direct operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that when there is a military operation, the officer who is in charge of the operation is located in a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he will have all his maps and relevant information so he can direct operations and a communication system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is this some rule that is in force in all the armies in the world? Or was this something specific to the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Forward command post is a standard procedure for most operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, may I ask you when did you see this document, if at all, for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not in dispute that the witness didn't see this document before. This was stated yesterday, when Mr. Karnavas was questioning the witness but we are talking about the contents and the events linked to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Lane, if you know, when this document was issued on the 24th of January, a Colonel Stewart, General Morillon, were they in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, did you ever visit Colonel Siljeg at the forward command post there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will now show you some documents that followed before you went to Gornji Vakuf and the peace negotiations. Let us begin with document P 1329. It's a document that has already been admitted into evidence. It is a joint statement by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, dated the 27th of January 1993, compiled in Geneva. It's a brief document. You can see it. I just wish to draw your attention to the concluding part of this joint statement. Did you know that Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban informed the commanders of the ABiH and the HVO, and they directed them to solve difficulties and to immediately set up a joint command? And I'm particularly interested in this joint command. Did you know that there was a political agreement on the formation of a joint command?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that a document had -- a joint document had been issued like this. I cannot remember, however, whether the con -- whether I was aware of the contents as I see them now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, please look at document P 1322. It's a document with the same date, issued by my client, General Petkovic, on the basis of this joint command whereby all operative activities are being banned but what we are particularly interested in that at the level of operative zones, contact be established with the appropriate commands of the ABiH with a view to setting up joint commands. Were you a witness of these activities at the end of January 1993, when these joint commands were being formed at regional levels and at higher levels?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, at that stage, I was in Gornji Vakuf. There was no joint commands being formed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to documents relating to Gornji Vakuf. Let us look at P 1341, please. It's a document dated the 28th of January, issued by General Petkovic, and in agreement with representatives of the 4th Corps of the ABiH, that a coordinating body be set up consisting of representatives of the army and the HVO at the level of the zone of operations of southeastern Herzegovina and the 4th Corps. An identical order was issued by Arif Pasalic, and it is a document you can find under number 4D 366. Tell me, please, did you know that Milivoj Petkovic and Arif Pasalic issued orders on the same days to form a coordinating body at the level of the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we are approaching the issue of Gornji Vakuf. So look at document P 1467, please. We are coming to discussions with Sefer Halilovic now. It is an order dated the 11th of February 1993, and I will summarise it but you can read it through. Agreement is being reached at the level of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH and the operative zone of the HVO Central Bosnia to form a coordinating team and the names are Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic. Under paragraph 2 it says, "The existing coordinating team of the ABiH and the HVO in Gornji Vakuf shall carry out the same assignments and its sphere of authority shall include Bugojno." Point 3 talks about Mostar. Point 4 says, "All the coordinating teams mentioned are charged with the task of preparing a proposal for the composition of joint commands in the areas of responsibility on the basis of the agreement reached by Izetbegovic and Boban." Tell us, Mr. Lane, please, whether you were a witness of all these efforts to form coordinating bodies at the level of various operative zones and at the level of the whole of Herceg-Bosna. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that you met General Petkovic at a meeting on the 30th [as interpreted] of January 1993 in Mostar and you also mentioned that with him and Arif Pasalic, you drove in your vehicles towards Gornji Vakuf. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this joint trip with General Petkovic to Gornji Vakuf took place on the 13th of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All I can do is to refer to the testimony of Mr. Christopher Beese, page 3102 of the transcript, where, in lines 14 to 18 he speaks of his trip to Gornji Vakuf on the 13th of February mentioning you, General Petkovic, and Arif Pasalic. Tell us, please, whether you know that General Petkovic stayed only for one day in Gornji Vakuf on that occasion and that all further discussions on the signing of an agreement he left to his associates?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague has drawn attention to an error in the transcript, page 39 [as interpreted], line 13, my question related to the 19th of January 1993 in Mostar, so I would like to correct the transcript accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have prepared, Mr. Lane, another document, P 1481, which was also prepared for you by the Prosecution for your examination-in-chief and he probably changed his mind when you said you couldn't remember those agreements, but let's have a look at them now. It's an agreement dated the 13th of February signed by Zrinko Tokic, and then there is another agreement of the 7th of February signed by Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, you have just announced a correction on page 39. That's what the transcript says. On page 39, Mr. Praljak is actually interrogating the witness. So probably the page is erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It should be page 69. I'm sorry. I wasn't following the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I can understand that very, very well. It's no criticism. Just an attempt to assist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for assistance. That was how I took it anyway, as assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to Mr. Siljeg. You said that you were most concerned by the fact that Mr. Siljeg did not come to those negotiations. The Prosecutor showed you a document on Monday, the number is P 1303, you don't need to look at it. I have nothing to ask you about it. This document says that Colonel Siljeg left the meeting because he was informed about the two soldiers having been killed and then he came the next day not in the morning but in the afternoon. Can you nevertheless confirm that Colonel Siljeg did take part in those negotiations and he did sign the agreements reached with the representatives of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're mixing up two things here. I never said Colonel Siljeg did not come to negotiations. What I said was when we were going through the final cease-fire agreements, he failed to show for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I must admit I can't understand quite what you said.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, if I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No. There is no need really, Mr. Lane. I have very little time left and document P 1303, it is stated why Colonel Siljeg left and that he came back the next day. So there isn't a single document that Colonel Siljeg should have signed and he didn't sign; is that right? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us which document was it that he could have signed and he didn't?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cease-fire arrangement, the documentation which was prepared by Mr. Beese on the 16th of February, was not signed by Mr. -- Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, the cease-fire agreement was signed at a far higher level, and now it was just a matter of implementation and execution. I'd like to now go on to another subject I'd like to return to Colonel Siljeg if we have time. There is a matter that I think is of much importance. You told us that the ABiH was more prepared to cooperate and more willing to put an end to the conflict whereas in your opinion the HVO wasn't really interested in a cease-fire. I'd now like to show you some ABiH documents that relate to the day when you spoke to HVO representatives in Mostar on the 19th of January 1993. And also, when you were trying to negotiate a cease-fire and an implementation of the agreement. First of all, could you have a look at P1210? It's a document drafted by Selmo Cikotic from the ABiH brigade in Gornji Vakuf. It's dated the 19th of January 1993. It's a special combat report addressed to the commander of the 3rd Corps. We can read through some parts of the document together. I'll just read out what I consider to be important. Under item 1, Mr. Lane, tell us, did you ever have the opportunity of meeting Selmo Cikotic? Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he is, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the local commander on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. The ABiH, that's clear. Item 1, Mr. Cikotic says that in combat to date they have lost the villages of Uzricje, Dusa, the lower part of Hrasnice, and a location where the relay on Strmica was located was lost. Mr. Lane, as a professional soldier, if someone says in a combat report something to this effect, does this mean that the ABiH was in the villages of Uzricje, Dusa, Hrasnice and at the Strmica feature and after combat it lost those areas? Is that what this paragraph in this document means?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Item 2, on that day when you were in Mostar agreeing on a cease-fire with the HVO and trying to find a peaceful solution to the conflict, the ABiH said, "The plan is to execute sabotage actions in the course of the night and to do so in several actions." I won't now mention the axes mentioned. In item 3, Selmo Cikotic tells -- makes certain requests which he addresses to his corps commander. We can see that they are in fact requesting assistance from Bugojno, they want help with the artillery that is to shell certain targets. They are requesting help from Konjic and Novi Travnik and they are requesting that the mujahedin help them. You can see that item number 1 mentions the mujahedin. Mr. Lane, did you know that in the area of Gornji Vakuf, the ABiH was massing its forces and preparing for certain combat operations and that concerns the day on which were you speaking to Arif Pasalic and Mr. Prlic and my client, General Petkovic in Mostar? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at P 1214. The Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Sefer Halilovic has addressed this document to Arif Pasalic. This was at the time that you spoke to Arif Pasalic and it says that, given the situation in Gornji Vakuf, it's necessary to take the following measures. The Neretvica Brigade and adequate forces from Prozor are to be engaged in order to take Makljen. Makljen is the pass that you have already referred to, isn't that the case, Mr. Lane?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us, did you know that the ABiH on the 19th of January 1993 was planning to take Makljen?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading this order and to answer your question, no. I'm reading the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Have a look at 4D 360. It's on the following day. It concerns the engaging the Neretvica Brigade. Arif Pasalic issue as order to the commander of the 7th Konjic Brigade and to the commander of the Neretvica brigade and again given the situation in Gornji Vakuf he orders that the Neretvica Brigade together with the units of the Prozor Battalion take the Makljen Pass. In brackets, Here, Sciti and Kute are also mentioned. Do you know those place names, Mr. Lane? Have you ever heard of these names? Do you know what they refer to?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, would you just repeat those names?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In brackets, you can see the following names. It's under item 1 in brackets, you can see Here, Sciti, it should read Scipe but it says Sciti, and then you have Kute. Do you know what these features are, are they villages, hills?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I knew them in 1992 but I forget now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. These are the names of villages. This order shows that Arif Pasalic, pursuant to an order from his superior, ordered his men to go into the field and to capture Makljen. Can we agree on that, Mr. Lane?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the -- as I read the order that's it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can skip some of the documents. Have a look at another document now. P 1226. It's on the same day. Enver Hadzihasanovic, the 3rd Corps commander is reporting to the staff of the BH armed forces. We can read through, we can all read through the document. I'd like to discuss the last section of the document, the fifth line from the bottom in the B/C/S. Or rather it's the end of the first page in English. It says the upper part of the town and all the villages inhabited by Muslims are under the control of the army, apart from the village of Uzricje, from which some of the residents have voluntarily evacuated and moved to Gornji Vakuf as well as to the village of Hrasnice, whose residents have been evacuated to Grnica. Mr. Lane, does this ABiH report show that the Muslim inhabitants voluntarily left the village of Uzricje and moved to Gornji Vakuf? And that is also the case for the village of Hrasnice? Is this something that we can conclude on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While he is reading the document, we could have our 20-minute break now. We will resume at 6.00 p.m. Ms. Alaburic, you ever another 30 minutes at your disposal, in principle, but we'll have to calculate the time, and the Prosecution will have its 30 minutes for re-examination. So we should be able to conclude by the end of the day. Sir, you have read the document now. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I took you up wrong there. I thought what you meant was I would bring the document with me for the break and read it during the break. I apologise. I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would be very grateful if the witness could read all the other documents that are in my bundle, the ones we haven't discussed yet. It will be easier for the next stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. During the 20-minute break you can have a rest by reading the documents. We'll resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Ms. Alaburic, the registrar has done the necessary calculations and he has informed me that that you have used up an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wanted to -- you probably have noticed that Mr. Kovacic is absent from the Court and he indicated he wanted me to pass along just in case you haven't been apprised, that he is feeling rather sick and so that's why he's not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I hope he will be well soon. Ms. Alaburic, you have used up your time. We'll grant you another five minutes to conclude so that we are fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I could be granted a little more time, I appreciate that, but it's for you to decide whether the subjects are of importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I want to finish asking you questions about this document. I know you're interested in others parts of the document but I'd like you to tell me something about the two villages mentioned in this report drafted by Enver Hadzihasanovic, these villages from which the Muslim inhabitants left on a voluntary basis. Is that what we can conclude on the basis of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, I apologise, could I get the exhibit number for this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. P 01226.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, as a professional soldier, when you read through the report of another professional soldier, is this a conclusion one can draw?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if the translation "arbitrary evacuation" is a correct translation from the Serbo-Croat, if I'm reading the right thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "The upper part of the town and all the villages inhabited by Muslims under the ABiH control apart from the villages -- apart from the village of Uzricje, from which part of the population left on a voluntary basis and they moved to Gornji Vakuf." That's the case for the village of Hrasnica and the population was evacuated from that village to Grnica.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not being difficult here. I apologise for this. Maybe I'm just getting tired but could you just point me in the direction of the word "voluntary" in that document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic -- voluntarily, what you're saying is important. Can you read down the paragraph in your own language because the English translation is problematic, I believe. So I would like to you read out the paragraph in your own language, the paragraph that relates to the inhabitants of the village, the inhabitants who left their village. Could you read it out in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just done that. It's on the page that is on the screen now from line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please reread it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. "The upper part of the town and all the villages inhabited by Muslims are under the control of the Armija, of the army, apart from the village of Uzricje, from which some of the residents have moved out voluntarily." I'll end the quote. I don't believe the interpretation is correct because it doesn't say, "some of the residents," it says, "Part of" perhaps we could be more literal. I'll recommence, "The other part of the town and all the villages inhabited by Muslims are under the control of the Armija apart from the village of Uzricje, from which a part of the residents have voluntarily moved out and moved to Gornji Vakuf. As well as the village of Hrasnica, whose residents have been evacuated to Grnica." So the word "samovoljno" has been translated as arbitrarily. And I think that's a correct translation. It's been translated as voluntarily, not arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I had some doubts about the translation, I wanted to you read it out in your own language and translation introduces the idea of voluntarily. That means that the villagers left these two villages voluntarily. It means that they weren't controlled. They weren't forced to do so. That's the correct translation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, I don't think we have to linger on this document now. I'd like to clarify something about the military leadership in Herceg-Bosna. Did you know that Mate Boban was the supreme commander of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have known in 1992 but I don't know today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you have told us that my client, General Petkovic, had control over his subordinates, which is why I have to ask you whether you believe that he had control over each and every soldier and each and every officer of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every officer is responsible for what his soldiers do and fail to do. It's one of the principles of being a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, I'm not talking about responsibility. I'm asking you about control now. You established that General Petkovic had control over his subordinates and now I want to ask you something about your claim. First of all, I would like to ask you whether you had control over all soldiers, all officers and all HVO units in the territory of Herceg-Bosna in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I had in mind were the people who report directly to him in his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who these people were, the people who were directly accountable to him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is General Petkovic worked in a structure and he had a certain position in that structure. Everybody underneath him, he was responsible for. I don't know what the structure was and I can't remember who was under him. But he is responsible for those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, I'd like to draw your attention to the following again. We are not discussing responsibility or the chain of command. We are referring to your claim that he had control over his subordinates. Tell me, did you believe that he had real and effective control or does the concept of control have a different meaning for you?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Control/responsibility. It's a military definition we are talking about here and we are talking about the chain of command. That's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you then did not have real and effective control in mind, you didn't have specific events in mind, events for which he had control? You were thinking of control in terms of chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic is part of a military structure, as I am, and as I repeat, every officer is responsible for what his subordinates do or fail to do. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's not in dispute, Mr. Lane. We are now just trying to analyse your claim, which has much weight in these proceedings, and that claim concerns the fact that General Petkovic had control over his subordinates. My task is to clarify the sort of control you were referring to when you made that claim.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is responsible for the effective, efficient administration and operational activity of his people. That's the control.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But control and responsibility are matters that need to be distinguished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer the question now and we will then conclude. The Judges are becoming impatient. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honour, in the military system, a military officer is vested with responsibility/control for his subordinates. That's exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, that concludes your examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just put one concluding question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, your conclusion according to which General Petkovic had control over his subordinates, can you tell me the factual basis upon which you drew such a conclusion? Apart from the fact that he occupied a certain position within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that is the whole point of what I'm saying. He was a general in a military structure. That gives him responsibilities that he has to ensure that he applies in a pure, effective, fair manner. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if we could then agree on this, your claim concerns the position he occupied within the HVO chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. He's a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, thank you. I am sorry we didn't have more time and I would like to thank the Judges for granting me additional time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, while you've got those documents there with you, I want to take you to a couple of those first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't forget that re-examination has to have a direct link to the cross-examination. That's always the case. So to avoid any questions, you should say, "When answering such and such a question, you said such and such a thing. And now I have this document to show you and so on and so forth." We need a basis and then an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, Ms. Alaburic showed you Exhibit P 1214 and asked you some questions about a couple of items in that, 1214. Do you have that document with you?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a document of the Armija directed to the 4th Corps commander, Mr. Pasalic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted ask you a couple of questions about this first paragraph. Second sentence says, "The attack on the -- and the attack of the HVO units on the city," referring to Gornji Vakuf, "is carried out from the direction of Prozor, from the area of Makljen Pass." Is that consistent with your own observations from having been up there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Continues: "There are still no infantry attacks on the city but the city and our defenders are under fire from all -- from all artillery weapons." Again, the fighters or defenders here being those of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that sentence also consistent with the observations that you made when you arrive?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Next sentence continues: "HVO forces were brought from Tomislavgrad, Livno and other towns in Herzegovina." Is that consistent with the briefings and the information that was available to you at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The next document that I want to take you to is one that was also just shown to you by Ms. Alaburic. It's 1266. P 01266. And --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon. P 0?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P 01266. I think it's just the document behind the one that you were just looking at. 1266?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1266.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it's here but I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm saying it wrong. 1226. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 19th of January 1993. And again it's an Armija, army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, document, SITREP for Gornji Vakuf, 19 January. The first sentence makes reference to an ultimatum which had expired. Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the subordination of the Armija forces to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then it continues, the HVO launched an all-out attack on Gornji Vakuf on the 18th of January at 0300 hours. Is that consistent with the information that you were -- that you were receiving at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And that the attack was using all available means tanks, howitzers, MB, I'm not sure what that is, armoured transport, PAM, answer aircraft machine-gun, et cetera. Based on what you saw, were those -- with the exception of the chemical agents, which I'll ask you about but the other items, the other types of weaponry, were those -- is that consistent with what you were observing once you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot itemise the different natures of equipment used but I know there was artillery and rockets fired. I cannot give designations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know or did you hear, were you briefed at all, about whether any chemical weapons were being used in the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then the next line, again troops which the HVO drew from Prozor were deployed in the region of couple of locations and then there is a reference to Makljen again and additional locations. I know that you're not going to know all those places but again at least in respect of Makljen --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- is that consistent with what your information was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Could I direct you to another exhibit that was shown to you on the cross-examination just a little while ago? Exhibit 1211, 1211. It's also in the binder. This is an order emanating from Mr. Mate Boban dated 19th of January to the head of the Defence department, chief of the HVO Main Staff. So at this time, on the 19th of January 1993, do you know what this order was directed to? Who was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume it was General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who was the head of the Defence department at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So now, with Mr. Boban issuing an order to Mr. Stojic and General Petkovic, is that consistent with the chain of command as you understood it to exist at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. You can put that away. Now, I want to take you back now to some -- a couple of the items or issues that were raised during your cross-examination yesterday, and the first of those relates to -- I know there were a couple of questions that came up, I think, from Mr. Karnavas and also Mrs. -- Well, I don't want to misstate it but I'm going to ask you about your interpreter, the first interpreter that you hired, Ms. Zvoko [sic]?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zovko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Because you were asked who or how did you decide or learn who were the people that you should talk to when you first arrived in Siroki Brijeg, and you indicated that it was this interpreter Ms. Zovko who was one of the first or who was actually a source of information on that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was absolutely, and she introduced me to, as I said, key leaders, pointed me in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And would that include Mr. Prlic, Stojic and the others that you testified --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I would have been briefed about men -- these very important people at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. What was her nationality or her ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was Australian and she was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And did she bear a relationship to the priest in Siroki Brijeg who you testified about?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. She was related to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you just a brief question or two about the map or the drawing that was -- you were asked about on the cross-examination by Mr. Karnavas. He took you to paragraph 47 of your witness statement and the question that I have on that is -- you were asked where is the drawing or was it given to you? And I don't know who actually physically made the drawing, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And is there anything particular about how he made the drawing that you recall as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just remember being surprised at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. What did he use to make the drawing?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And anything in particular you remember about that beyond what you've already said?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some sort of a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A ballpoint pen, a fountain pen, a good pen, what kind of pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very good pen, good quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of a Swiss brand?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, also during your cross-examination by Mr. Karnavas, he took you to paragraph 37 of your witness statement or your OTP witness statement, I should say, and he read that to you and I want to just also read that same part to you and ask you to clarify something. What the statement says is this: "I attended a number of meetings of the Presidency of the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I noticed during the meetings that Mr. Prlic was the most significant personality at these meetings even though Mr. Boban would chair the meeting, he had very little input into the deliberations." And then Mr. Karnavas then asked a couple of questions about the Presidency, what you understood that to be, the meetings, and also the self-proclaimed part of the title. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. My question is this: Whether, as indicated here, whether it is in fact your evidence that at these meetings, Mr. Prlic was the most significant personality and that -- well, I'll just leave it at that, whether as indicated here Mr. Prlic was the most significant personality at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then -- excuse me, Mr. President. You were taken to paragraph 112 of your statement, and this part was read to you and then you were invited to -- there was part of it that you withdrew, that you wanted to withdraw, and I wanted to clarify what you were withdrawing and what you're not withdrawing. And this is the part that was read to you on cross-examination: "In my professional opinion, that throughout my period of time in the area of operations, the Republic of Croatia was a major influence both politically and militarily with the Bosnian Croats and their activity." And then was continued: "On many occasions," again this is from your statement now. "On many occasions I saw military hardware with Croatian army designation and military personnel wearing the uniform of the Croatian army." Continuing: "I believe that the Bosnian Croats saw no future for the Bosnian Muslims. There is no doubt that the influence of the European Union and the future ambitions of people like Boban and Jadranko Prlic ensured that these people were very conscious of not upsetting the European Union. However, they had contempt for the United Nations." And then counsel continued on the same theme taking you to paragraph 45 of your statement where he made reference to Mr. Boban and his cohorts wanting to live in a Greater Croatia as a society based on Catholicism, and then again, as indicated in your statement: "It appeared to me that their major political direction was unification with the Republic of Croatia." So now you were asked about all that and I wanted to make sure the record is clear what your evidence is on that in terms of what you're withdrawing and what you're not withdrawing. Is it your evidence that in your opinion, based on the period of time you spent in the area, that the Republic of Croatia was a major influence both politically and militarily with the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I understand correctly, then it was your intent to withdraw the next sentence which says, "On many occasions, I saw military hardware with Croatian army designation and military personnel wearing the uniform of the Croatian army." Is that -- do you stay with that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the withdrawal -- the part you wanted to correct or modify then related I think more to the Croatian army equipment, tanks and whatnot?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Because you didn't see any Croatian army tanks, I think is -- all right. It continues, "I believe that the Bosnian Croats saw no future for the Bosnian Muslims." Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then, the passage about Boban and Prlic ensuring that the people were -- that they did not want to upset the European Union but they had contempt for the United Nations. Is that still your evidence or --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the word "contempt" was a bit strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The reference to the United Nations there, I wasn't sure, I mean that's a pretty --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then finally, whether you were withdrawing or modifying or standing by your evidence as to whether Mr. Boban and his cohorts wanted to live in a Greater Croatia, a society based on Catholicism and a the major direction was unification with the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just intervene here Mr. Stringer because your question was termed differently from the statement. You said they wanted to live in and here it says they were living in. Perhaps you would wish to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I will. I'm actually reading from the transcript of the Court hearing yesterday when the statement was read back and I should probably just be reading directly from the statement. This is paragraph 45, I believe. "Mr. Boban and his cohorts were of the opinion that they were living in Greater Croatia as a society based on Catholicism with very little interest in other ethnic groups such as the Muslims. It appeared to me that their major political direction was unification with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, are you still of that view or was -- is that the view that you reached based on your experience in the region?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked by counsel for Mr. Prlic and then also I believe counsel for Mr. Stojic about the situation with the refugees at the gym in Posusje, and you were specifically asked who did you contact about getting aid in there? Did you --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, as far as I know, I didn't ask any questions about Posusje. I don't think that that is particularly important, but let the record be clear. I talked about aid to Stolac, not about Posusje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, is there a mistake there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at page 23849 of the transcript yesterday. At line 11, the witness says that he's referring to Stolac, Posusje, Gradska and other areas and he's talking about the situation of humanitarian aid and then moving down to line 20, counsel says, "You haven't asked my question. I'm asking, I'm talking about the distribution of humanitarian aid that did reach the Muslims coming from UNHCR to Eastern Mostar." And then the question is by counsel on line 23: "My question was whether you were aware of the way in which the humanitarian aid was distributed, did you have any information about the distribution?" So I believe -- I interpreted that to include Posusje because the witness had mentioned a couple of different locations. But I don't think it actually affects my question and I'll withdraw it to the extent that --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm glad that the colleague has read this out because this related to humanitarian aid to East Mostar. I remember that I had no questions about Posusje and what my learned friend has just read confirms that, but he has withdrawn the question so I don't think that is important any longer. I just wanted to say that I was sure about what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to withdraw the question but I -- it's my position that the issue of the humanitarian aid distribution to the refugees at the Posusje gym was raised. I know it was discussed on the cross-examination by Mr. Karnavas and I'd like to ask just one question to follow-up on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before the question is asked I would like a foundation because timing is important. And whether the gentleman knew at the time how much aid was actually available to provide, who was in control of that aid, who was distributing and so on and so forth. So I think that there is some foundation, but I'll listen to the question, I'll be glad to object if I need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. It's much more specific actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that is this, Witness: Do you recall, did you or any of your people actually go down to Posusje and make any observations about the distribution or non-distribution of humanitarian aid to the people in that gym?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said in testimony that we carried out an investigation of Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what did that investigation involve?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was an urgent requirement for humanitarian aid to be brought to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Did you send anyone down there to observe whether they were getting the aid that they needed?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent a vehicle down on a number of nights to see where, if there was humanitarian aid there, where was it actually going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what did they find?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found a number of military vehicles leaving the location with this aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what group or military organisation these vehicles belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my redirect. As I indicated yesterday it was my intention to just tender into evidence the witness's statement based upon the questions that were put to him, the parts of it that were read out to him, not just by Mr. Karnavas but it was gone into extensively by the other accused as well in cross-examination and so it is my intention to tender the statement itself into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard briefly on that and I'm glad this was raised now: The Prosecution can't have it both ways. They can't decide to bring a witness viva voce and then try to tender a statement and after they do, their direct -- full-blown direct examination, to avail themselves to another procedure that was available to them at the time. That's first and foremost and now I'm talking about 92 ter. They have in the past and I'm sure this was a tactical or strategic decision on their part. I think that it wouldn't be personal for me to say that between the two senior trial lawyers they have 50 years of experience so I doubt if they make decisions on the fly, you know, as it were. So they made a tactical decision to bring the gentleman in, first of all. Second of all, portions of the statement were not discussed at all on direct examination, nor were they covered on cross-examination. Thirdly, the portions that were discussed on cross-examination obviously, I think, those specific paragraphs can indeed come in. That would be the normal procedure, especially since they go to the veracity of this particular individual. Part of the essence of the cross-examination was not so much to challenge the witness, although that was -- that did occur, to challenge his memory, not necessarily for his veracity but just memory in particular, but was to show that the manner in which the statement was taken, especially where the gentleman had to withdraw, or he vividly recalled seeing Mr. Prlic being in a meeting where Mr. Prlic said that he had issued an order, and that was withdrawn, and this was on the basis of being shown a document. The purpose of that, Your Honours, was to show the technique that is involved by the Office of the Prosecution investigators in order to suggest or encourage a memory. Documents need to be shown to revive a memory or to refresh a memory, but in some instances, the unintended result may be, as it was here, to actually create a memory, it created a memory which at least this gentleman, thanks to the lovely beaches of Scheveningen, during his jog was able to recollect that, yes, indeed, he was not at that meeting and therefore could not vouch for what, if anything, was said by Dr. Prlic, a very, very critical point. So part of the cross-examination, the technique, as it were, was to demonstrate the dangerousness of simply accepting statements when they are prepared in the fashion in which they are.
