They are not question and answer, question and answer. They are not taken by an objective participant. They are taken by a party. Those are the rules. They are not taken by an investigative judge or even a Prosecutor, say, from a civil law system where they are bound, duty-bound, to ask all of the exculpatory questions as well and to collect all that evidence. That's why -- that was the essence. But I don't think that the Prosecution can now stand up and say they want to tender the entire statement. If that is in fact the case, since we don't have at least a witness for Monday or Tuesday, you know, and we have to -- at least we are free for tomorrow the gentleman would need to stay here and then we need to give myself, including my colleagues, an opportunity to take a second bite at the apple as well to cover the areas which weren't covered, and I know for a fact that I was able to receive time at least from the Coric Defence, and from the Pusic Defence that they ceded their time to me because based on the direct examination, there was no need. Now, with the statement coming in, I dare say, not only do I need to spend at least an additional hour with the gentleman, but I'm sure my colleagues would, no doubt, wish to do the same and we need to go into certain other areas because, as I noted, Mr. President, during the briefing session, the proofing session, and again, that wasn't tape recorded but we did receive a detailed account of all the corrections and that was the whole purpose by the way of why I did such a meticulous, if I could use that word with your permission, attempt to show how the gentleman is careful, how he reads, how he prepares his orders and the daily reports to show that he read the statement at the time and yet we have all these errors, including his own title. That was the whole purpose of all of that. So I think, if we are now going to tender all the statement in, because there are other errors as well that I didn't go into because they are not necessary, they are not relevant to this particular case or to the case that I'm having to answer which was the Prosecution's direct examination, I would object. I think this -- we are going into a new procedure and if this is the case, that now the Prosecution can do the direct and then, if the Defence refers to any portions of the statement, the statement can then come in, then I think we need to revisit the rules and we need to rewrite the rules. Because I think we are going into a 92 ter approach with full viva voce for the Prosecution and they simply cannot have it both ways. And let me just end with one note, a lesson that I learned from the Blagojevic case taught to me by none ore other than the Presiding Judge, Judge Liu. It was the second or third witness. I didn't get to ask all my questions and I moved for the admission of the statement, the entire statement, at which point I was reminded and properly so, that that is not the procedure here. That if I want something from a particular statement into the record I need to ask it but the whole statement simply doesn't come in, and I think that's the lesson that should be learned here. But the Prosecution need not leave -- learn anything because they know this already, and even if we were in our own national jurisdictions with the federal rules of evidence, I'm sure the Prosecution would agree with me that he could not tender the entire statement in. He could tender the portions, the paragraphs, which were directly brought up on cross-examination. In fact, it would be the defence that would be offering that as substantive evidence because those were used to impeach the witness. Now, I don't know if my colleagues wish to chime in. I believe my colleague for the Coric team and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we do, as it happens. Well, the Petkovic Defence, we certainly support Mr. Karnavas's submissions that this should be excluded except, and that is the answer, except that very limited extent which Mr. Karnavas has identified. Of course, the particular passages which were referred to in cross-examination have to be admitted to make sense of the cross-examination. It's really as simple as that, but beyond that, in a nutshell, this is an attempt to add wholesale to the examination-in-chief when we are right at the end. We just had the cross-examination. We've just had the re-examination. So we would be starting all over again with this major addition to examination-in-chief. That's simply can't be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours, the application of my learned friend is vigorously opposed on behalf of Bruno Stojic. Your Honour, in assessing the merits of the Prosecution application one must, of course, have in mind the scale of the statement and the nature and length of cross-examination on the alleged inconsistencies or the scope of the cross-examination. Your Honour, in this matter, the statement is about 20 pages. In fact, I depart with respect from my learned friend's submission that there is even a need for extracts to be put in before Your Honours. I don't object if it's done but the normal course, of course, the normal procedure is that counsel read into evidence in the course of the cross-examination, you said X, and now you say Y. But, Your Honour, if the statement in toto is to be put into evidence, we would, with the greatest of respect, but also with the greatest of force, request that the witness remain and be further cross-examined. Your Honours, I have just walked into this case and Your Honours of course will make their own assessment as to the conduct of each counsel in this case but certainly from what I understand and from what I've seen, at least lead counsel for Mr. Stojic has endeavoured wherever possible to put forward very focused cross-examination and that, of course, is predicated upon the evidence that is elicited by the Prosecution in its case in chief. If the Defence have to cross-examination on a whole plethora of documents and a whole variety of different matters averred to in a statement, these proceedings will never end and, Your Honour, we would be prejudiced significantly. So I do urge and it is our submission that the Prosecution's application should be denied as being unnecessary. To the extent that Your Honours are against me on that, we would ask that the witness remain here and be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall be very brief. I join my colleagues in everything that they have already said, and I would especially underline on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Coric, as Mr. Karnavas had said, that we based our decision not to cross-examine this witness on the basis of the direct examination. If we knew that there was a possibility for the statement to be admitted, then we would have opted for cross-examination. But not knowing that such a statement could be admitted and it should be admitted, our client will be prejudiced and he will not have the right to ask this witness about parts of the statement that are of importance and relevant to him. Should the Chamber allow the statement to be admitted, we would ask for additional time as Mr. Karnavas has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I would just like to say something else. Mr. Stringer said, when he presented the foundation for the admission of the statement, he said because the decision [as interpreted] used it, but if we look at your decision of the 28th of April, that is our right. We are entitled to ask and refer to the statement to refresh his memory, so that cannot be a basis for asking for the statement to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I will give you the floor but listen to what I'm going to say. The Prosecution is obliged by the regulations which say that if you have a viva voce witness, you put questions, the witness answers, and you show him documents. Within that procedure, there is no admission of the written statement. So it is a choice to be made by the Prosecution. A second point: The Prosecution may now, thanks to me, resort to 92 ter and the Prosecution may choose in favour of a written statement and informs the parties in advance of making such a procedural choice, and this will gain time and then the Defence knows that it has to cross-examine on the whole document. You started with the viva voce testimony, and toward the end, you are now asking for the admission of the statement. And as Mr. Karnavas has said, you can't have it both ways. The Defence have expressed their legal positions. The Chamber has not deliberated. What would be your response to what has been said so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Based on my experience in the case I think the manner in which the cross-examination of this witness has been unique as compared to the other ones that I've seen and I think it did result -- it obviously resulted certainly in significant parts of the witness statement being read to the witness during his cross-examination, everybody agrees to that. However, I think that the point raised by counsel for Mr. Coric is well taken in that counsel for Mr. Coric, as well as counsel for Mr. Pusic, I know he doesn't figure in this quite as much, that they made a decision to cede their time to other accused and I think it's a point well taken. I would also add that the suggestion made by Mr. Karnavas and I think seconded by Mr. Stewart, that those portions of the statement that were read during the cross-examination, those specific paragraphs be tendered into evidence, and that -- those parts of the statement, together with the witness's testimony about them, would then be the evidence. And that would be acceptable to the Prosecution. So again, we would be tendering the paragraphs that were referred to during the cross-examination of the witness. And those only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're modifying now your request, joining on the whole the Defence positions, asking for the admission of only the paragraphs read by you or the Defence, so that is the position now. Of course, the Chamber will deliberate on the matter. So now, sir, your testimony has been completed. On behalf of my colleagues, I wish to thank you for coming at the request of the Prosecution and may I extend best wishes for your return to Dublin. I will ask the usher to be kind enough to lead you out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a few seconds we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 7.00 p.m. I thank everybody, and I wish you a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.
